actress_prominence: Female lead; the established star of the film, per Filmfare
initial_relationship: Fellow college students; she is the Police Commissioner's daughter and he is from a poor family
how_they_meet: At college, where Arjun falls in love with her.
courtship_pattern: Not described beyond his falling for her. Its one documented act is hers: when he is jailed for attacking a corrupt police officer, Deepa bails him out with her father's help, and her father then makes him a policeman.
emotional_dynamic: She is his patron as well as his love, the route by which an angry poor student becomes a respectable officer.
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between them is documented; the only recorded exchange is her rescuing him from jail.
external_opposition_explanation: The class gap between a commissioner's daughter and a tenement boy is real but meets no resistance, since her father sponsors him. The gangster Bhaiji's campaign is aimed at Arjun and his family rather than at the couple, and the summary never shows it touching Deepa.
lover_boy_explanation: A debut built on anger and muscle: he falls in love, but the role's identity is the honest officer against the gangster, and the romance is the means by which he enters the force.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Filmfare's retrospective treats Divya Bharti as the film's established star and Shetty as the debutant whose appeal was anger and muscle, which suggests an unequal pairing in screen presence; the score is held at the midpoint for want of any assessment.
actor_transformation: Her intervention converts a jailed brawler into a policeman, the only documented change the romance produces in him.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the Wikipedia summary ends with Arjun framed and arrested, and Deepa does not reappear in it after his posting.
relationship_analysis: The debut sets out a structure the early films keep returning to: the woman of higher station whose family sponsors the hero's entry into respectability, while the real conflict is between him and a criminal. She acts more decisively than he does in the romance itself, bailing him out of jail, but the summary gives her nothing to do once the gangster plot begins.
critical_reading: No contemporary review was located. Read now, the romance is a vehicle for class patronage: the commissioner's daughter and her father convert the poor man's anger into state service, and the heroine's narrative work is finished once he is in uniform.

actress_prominence: Second female lead, paired with Shetty while Ayesha Jhulka pairs with Akshay Kumar
initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: On his first day in Mumbai, on his way to college, Sunil helps Mamta change her car's tyre by lifting the car; she is amazed by his strength and simplicity.
who_initiates: Mutual: her admiration comes first, and he falls in love after a chat in the college canteen
courtship_pattern: A chance roadside meeting and a canteen conversation, after which he is in love; the rest of the romance is carried by the terrorist plot, in which he takes Mamta with him to deliver the Crypton and later frees her from Chikara's men.
emotional_dynamic: Uncomplicated attraction to the country boy's strength, under the nerd's disguise his uncle has put him in.
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between them is recorded; the couple's only obstacle comes from outside.
external_opposition_explanation: Colonel Chikara's terrorists kidnap Vikas and Ayesha and force Sunil to deliver the Crypton; Mamta goes with him and is left in the gang's hands until Sunil and Vikas return to free her.
lover_boy_explanation: He falls in love quickly and fights for her, but the role's identity is the strongman disguised as a nerd and the action hero against the terrorists.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The meeting is a set piece built to sell his physique to her and to the audience, which gives the pairing a clear premise; with no account of how it played, the score is held at the midpoint.
actor_transformation: None documented; the romance confirms the strongman rather than changing him.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the film ends with Chikara dead and 'everybody' safe.
relationship_analysis: His first film with Akshay Kumar divides the romance in two, one heroine per hero, and gives Shetty's half the purest form of his early appeal: a woman impressed because he lifts a car. The disguise his uncle imposes is the only complication, and it is a joke rather than a deception between the lovers.
critical_reading: No review was located. The pairing is an action-comedy convenience, and Mamta's role is to admire, to be endangered and to be rescued.

actress_prominence: Female lead, paired with Ajay Devgn's Arun
initial_relationship: Vikram knows her first through Arun's story and a photograph in Arun's suitcase
how_they_meet: Not documented; the summary reveals only that Vikram 'also fell in love with Sapna' and kept it from Arun, then tracks her down to ask her to see Arun.
who_initiates: Vikram, silently; his love is never declared in the summary
courtship_pattern: None. His feeling is concealed and turned into service of the rival's love: he finds Sapna, arranges for her to see Arun without being seen, tells her the truth about Mama Thakur, and rescues her from Shankar Bihari before bringing her to Arun.
emotional_dynamic: Silent devotion redirected into restoring her to the man she loves.
pair_conflict: None between them; the conflict is inside Vikram, between his feeling and his loyalty to Arun.
pair_friction_explanation: Nothing passes between them that could produce friction: he never declares himself, and every documented act of his serves her reunion with Arun.
external_opposition_explanation: The decisive obstacle is her love for Arun, which Vikram never contests; Mama Thakur and Shankar Bihari endanger her as well, but they oppose Arun's romance, not his.
lover_boy_explanation: He is first the investigating officer, but the film's last image belongs to his renunciation, driving the reunited lovers with sadness and joy on his face. Renunciation is a lover-boy act, so the role scores higher than its screen romance would suggest.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The relationship is designed to stay unspoken, so its effect depends on his restraint in her presence rather than on any shared romantic scene; the score is held at the midpoint.
actor_transformation: None of his feeling survives into action except as service; he ends where he began, alone, having given her up.
female_transformation: Not applicable to this pairing; her arc runs through Arun.
relationship_outcome: He gives her up; the film ends with Vikram driving Arun and Sapna, sad that he too loved her and glad that Arun has her.
relationship_analysis: The first of the second-hero roles in which Shetty loves the heroine and serves the hero's romance. It earned him a Filmfare nomination for Best Supporting Actor, and its emotional weight is almost entirely in what he does not say.
critical_reading: No review was located. The film frames silent renunciation as nobility, and Sapna is never asked: she is the object of two men's loyalty to each other as much as of their love.

actress_prominence: Extended cameo, per the article's cast list; Raveena Tandon is the film's heroine, opposite Akshay Kumar
initial_relationship: Married before the film's present
how_they_meet: Not documented.
courtship_pattern: Not documented; the marriage exists in Vishal's backstory.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented beyond the marriage itself.
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between husband and wife is recorded.
external_opposition_explanation: Four criminals gang-rape and kill her sister Rita, are acquitted with a corrupt prosecutor's help, and then attempt to rape Priya, who dies by suicide. Outside violence ends the marriage in death.
lover_boy_explanation: His killing of the four men is an act for his wife and her sister, but the role is organised around vengeance and then around Jindal's manipulation; the marriage is the wound, not the identity.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Poonam Jhawer's part is an extended cameo confined to Vishal's past, so the pairing has little room to establish itself; the score is held below the midpoint for that reason, not on any assessment of the performances.
actor_transformation: Her death and the acquittal of the men responsible turn him into a murderer serving a life sentence, which is what makes him useful to Jindal.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: She dies by suicide after the acquitted men attempt to rape her; Vishal kills all four.
relationship_analysis: A backstory marriage whose destruction is the origin of the character. Mohra's romance belongs to Amar and Roma; Vishal's is over before the film starts, and its only function is to supply a grievance that Jindal can exploit.
critical_reading: The film uses sexual violence against two women, one raped and murdered and one driven to suicide, as the male protagonist's motive. Neither woman has a part beyond that function, a device modern criticism regards as one of the period's most persistent.

actress_prominence: Second female lead; the Commissioner's daughter, paired with Kishan while Shilpa Shirodkar plays Gopi's wife
initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the Police Commissioner's daughter and he a released convict hunting his father
how_they_meet: Not documented.
courtship_pattern: She falls in love with Kishan while he is secretly killing Sawant's goons and letting his look-alike Gopi take the credit; he later tells her the truth, and she agrees to help him recover the hidden loot.
emotional_dynamic: She is drawn to a man whose identity and mission she does not know; disclosure turns her into his ally.
pair_conflict: His concealment of who he is, resolved when he tells her.
pair_friction_explanation: The only strain is what he hides from her, and the summary records no quarrel over it: he tells her and she joins him.
external_opposition_explanation: Sawant's gang captures and tortures Kishan, and Gopi hunts him on the police's behalf; nothing in the summary shows her father or anyone else opposing the romance itself.
lover_boy_explanation: She pursues him; he is occupied with his father and Sawant. The romance is a subplot of a double-role action comedy.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The summary gives it one turn, from her infatuation to her complicity, which leaves little to judge; the score is held at the midpoint.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: From a commissioner's daughter infatuated with a stranger to an accomplice in his recovery of the loot.
relationship_outcome: Together at the end; the cast list names her Kishan's wife.
relationship_analysis: In a double-role film the romance belongs to the dangerous twin, while the timid twin already has a wife and child. Barkha is the active party throughout, falling for Kishan and then choosing to help him once she knows the truth.
critical_reading: No review was located. Her choice to help a convict retrieve stolen jewels is framed as loyalty, and the film turns the police commissioner's daughter into the outlaw's ally without comment.

actress_prominence: Female lead opposite Shetty; Shilpa Shirodkar is paired with Akshay Kumar
initial_relationship: Strangers; he is the cause of her blindness
how_they_meet: A stray shot from Michael's attack on Bakshi Jang Bahadur blinds Maria, a hotel dancer; wracked with guilt, he tends to her in secret.
courtship_pattern: Guilt-driven care becomes love; he vows to restore her sight and takes Tuti Shah's contract on Inspector Dharam Das in exchange for money for her eye surgery, a deal that turns out to be a trap.
emotional_dynamic: Atonement and devotion; the summary does not say whether she learns that he fired the shot.
pair_conflict: None documented between them; the burden is his guilt.
pair_friction_explanation: He conceals his responsibility for her blindness, but no conflict between them is recorded.
external_opposition_explanation: Tuti Shah exploits Michael's love to make him kill again, the police hunt him for two murders, and a bomb threatens Maria's life in the final battle; Michael dies saving her.
lover_boy_explanation: Love organises his choices: he kills for her surgery, joins the fight against Tuti, dies saving her and gives her his eyes. Only the hitman's frame keeps it below the top of the scale.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The relationship is built on a blinded woman's dependence on a man who hides his part in her injury, so it rests on his tenderness rather than on exchange between them; the score is held at the midpoint.
actor_transformation: From Tuti Shah's pawn to a man who redeems himself, joining his estranged friend and father against Tuti and dying for Maria.
female_transformation: She regains her sight through his donated eyes and, now able to see, 'envisions Michael before her'.
relationship_outcome: Michael is fatally injured saving her from the bomb and asks that his eyes be donated to her; the surgery succeeds.
relationship_analysis: The most purely devotional role of the early films, and the most self-sacrificing: a lover-boy reading inside an action thriller. Its moral economy is exact, the eyes he took returned by his death, and that symmetry is the whole of Maria's part.
critical_reading: Sukanya Verma called the film a 'shoddy rip-off' of John Woo's The Killer. Read now, Maria is an object of atonement who is acted on from first scene to last; the romance is about Michael's guilt and redemption, and her sight is the token of it.

initial_relationship: Already in love when the film opens
how_they_meet: Not documented; they are a couple when D'Costa first sees them on the beach.
courtship_pattern: Ravi works hard to earn enough for them to marry. D'Costa frames him the day before the wedding; during his two years in jail D'Costa befriends Mohini, who comes to like and respect him. On her pleas DCP Mishra secures Ravi's early release, and they marry.
emotional_dynamic: Steady loyalty under siege; her trust in the man stalking her is the one fissure, and the summary never shows it reaching Ravi.
pair_conflict: None documented between them.
pair_friction_explanation: Her growing regard for D'Costa while Ravi is in jail is the nearest strain, but the summary records no quarrel; she works for Ravi's release and later joins his trap.
external_opposition_explanation: A corrupt police inspector who covets Mohini frames Ravi on the eve of the wedding, keeps him in jail for two years, and keeps harassing the married couple even after he is suspended and ordered to stay 500 feet away.
lover_boy_explanation: The marriage is what he works for and what D'Costa attacks, so his revenge is in defence of the couple; but its means, studying law and photographing D'Costa's crimes, make the role a thriller lead as much as a romantic one.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film needs the couple's bond to be beyond doubt for D'Costa's obsession to read as menace rather than rivalry, and their final trap requires them to act in concert; the score credits that structure, not any account of the performances.
actor_transformation: Prison turns a struggling photographer into a self-taught prosecutor who uses his camera and the law against the man who framed him.
female_transformation: From a fiancee who comes to respect her lover's persecutor to a partner who uses his desire against him.
relationship_outcome: Married; D'Costa is jailed and killed by the men he once framed, and Ravi walks away with Mohini.
relationship_analysis: The cleanest early statement of the pattern in this batch: pair friction 2 against external opposition 9. The couple is never in conflict; the obstacle is a third man with a badge. Mohini's agency is real, from her pleas for his release to the staged seduction that catches D'Costa.
critical_reading: No review was located. The film is inspired by Unlawful Entry, and its climax has the heroine perform seduction as bait: her body is the couple's weapon, which the film frames as cleverness and a modern reading sees as the same objectification the villain practises.

initial_relationship: Lovers before his supposed death, when he was a trainee pilot
how_they_meet: Not documented; they were lovers before the film's events.
courtship_pattern: Not shown. The film's romantic movement is her refusal to believe he is dead, his denial when she finds him as Krishna, and his confession after he saves her from would-be rapists.
emotional_dynamic: Her faith against his enforced concealment.
pair_conflict: He denies being Sunil to protect his new identity; when the tattoo bearing her name seems missing from his arm, she leaves broken-hearted.
pair_friction_explanation: A temporary but painful misunderstanding of his making: he lies to her face about who he is, and she leaves believing she was wrong. It ends when he tells her the truth.
external_opposition_explanation: His false identity is forced on him by the criminals who used his instructor and by the minister Amar Prabhakar, and his life as Krishna puts him among dons who would kill him if recognised.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance gives the gangster role a buried past, but the role is organised around survival and then vengeance for his sister.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The relationship is played almost entirely as recognition and denial, which leaves little to judge; the score is held at the midpoint.
actor_transformation: None documented; the confession restores a relationship but does not change his course.
female_transformation: Her belief that he is alive, which everyone else has abandoned, is vindicated.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the film ends with Sunil beheading Amar and surrendering.
relationship_analysis: The romance is the trace of the man he was before the alias, kept alive by the woman who refuses to accept his death. She is the one person who sees through Krishna, which makes her the film's measure of what he has lost.
critical_reading: No review was located. A club dancer mourning a lost lover and rescued from attempted rape is a stock figure, and the summary gives Rashmi no part in the plot after his confession.

initial_relationship: His sweetheart in his home village
how_they_meet: When Raj and his mother visit the village, he meets his best friend Raghu and his love interest Suman; how they first met is not documented.
who_initiates: Not stated; India Today describes Suman as 'a sexually aggressive village belle'
courtship_pattern: A village romance that ends quickly in marriage, after which Raj joins the IPS and the couple move to the city.
emotional_dynamic: Her boldness against his rectitude, per India Today's description of her; the summary records nothing of their married life.
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between them is recorded.
external_opposition_explanation: Raghu's goons, sent to stop Raj exposing his counterfeiting, nearly kill him and murder his mother and Suman.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship and marriage occupy the first act; after her murder the role is pure revenge.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. India Today's Anupama Chopra dismisses both leads separately, Shetty looking 'comatose' and Karisma Kapoor 'gauche' as a 'sexually aggressive village belle', which suggests a mismatch between her energy and his inertness; the score leans low on that basis.
actor_transformation: Her murder turns a newly married officer into an avenger.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Suman is murdered with Raj's mother by Raghu's goons; Raj recovers under Dr. Pooja Malhotra's care and takes revenge.
relationship_analysis: The marriage exists to be destroyed. It follows the Mohra pattern of the early films, in which the wife's death supplies the hero's motive, and the second heroine, the doctor who nurses him, is given no romance with him in any source.
critical_reading: India Today's reviewer saw Suman as a 'sexually aggressive village belle', a characterisation the film offers as comic appeal. Her murder in the first act makes her a motive rather than a character.

actress_prominence: Female lead; the judge's sister and a police inspector
initial_relationship: Lovers when the film begins, unknown to her brother
how_they_meet: Not documented.
courtship_pattern: Not shown; Film Information states that 'Romance is absent'.
emotional_dynamic: Duty against attachment: she arrests the man she loves on her brother's eyewitness evidence.
pair_conflict: On her brother's instruction she arrests Sunil for murder, 'shocked but duty-bound'.
pair_friction_explanation: The arrest sets her badge against her lover, but it is duty imposed by the case rather than conflict between them, and the summary records no estrangement.
external_opposition_explanation: The don D.V.M. frames Sunil through a look-alike to humiliate the judge; her brother's testimony sends him to death row; she is kidnapped by D.V.M. in the climax.
lover_boy_explanation: The trade review's verdict that romance is absent is borne out by the summary: his role is the condemned man and fugitive, and the love affair is a premise rather than a thread.
chemistry_explanation: Film Information's trade review says flatly that 'Romance is absent' and that the heroine 'looks like a dummy' except in the climax; the pairing has no romantic scenes to carry chemistry.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: Not documented; the trade review says she 'gets to show her bravery only in the climax'.
relationship_outcome: Reunited after D.V.M. is killed.
relationship_analysis: A romance that exists to give the judge a personal stake and the heroine a dilemma, then disappears until the final reunion. Its one strong scene on paper, a policewoman arresting her lover, is not developed in either source.
critical_reading: The trade press judged the heroine wasted: a police inspector in name who 'looks like a dummy'. The film gives her a profession with agency and then no use for it.

actress_prominence: Female lead, in a double role as Neha and her look-alike Rashmi
initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: He, a high-fashion photographer, 'bumps into' Neha, an actress-wannabe 'with high morals and therefore no roles' (India Today).
courtship_pattern: Brief: they fall in love and soon marry. The honeymoon in America is where the plot begins.
emotional_dynamic: Newlywed devotion; the film's emotional engine is his helplessness after she is taken.
pair_conflict: None.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between them is recorded; they are separated within the first act.
external_opposition_explanation: Neha is kidnapped from a restaurant washroom on their honeymoon by Vinod Kumar, who threatens her into proving him innocent of a murder, and replaced by a look-alike in a foreign country.
lover_boy_explanation: The whole plot is a husband's search for his wife, and the sources stress his devotion and helplessness; the action-man turn in the second half shifts the role toward the thriller.
chemistry_explanation: India Today's review captions the two leads 'The Shetty duo: Endearingly wooden' and finds that his 'trauma and helplessness don't come alive'; the pairing is likeable but inert, and the score reflects that.
actor_transformation: A fashion photographer becomes, overnight, an action hero hunting for his wife, a change India Today found unconvincing.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: He finds Neha and kills Vinod; they 'live happily ever after'.
relationship_analysis: A marriage that is complete before the plot begins and serves as the stake of a kidnapping thriller. The look-alike device doubles the heroine without giving either woman much to do.
critical_reading: India Today noted the film's chest-thumping about Indianness, Shetty raving against America, 'where women are kidnapped and morals' decline. The kidnapping of a wife is made into an argument about national virtue, with Neha as the evidence.

actress_prominence: Female lead; second-billed after Shetty in the article
initial_relationship: Daughter of the lawyer who helps Kundan move to Mumbai
how_they_meet: Through her father, the lawyer Satyaprakash, who helps Kundan and his brother settle in Mumbai.
courtship_pattern: Not described; they marry after Kundan becomes 'Bhai', and name their son Kisna after his murdered brother.
emotional_dynamic: She stands for the domestic life that his vendetta endangers, while her sister Meenu supports his operations.
pair_conflict: Her fear that his criminal activities will endanger him and the family.
pair_friction_explanation: A recurring worry rather than a rupture: she fears what his life will do to them, and nothing records her acting against it.
external_opposition_explanation: The gangsters David and Malik and the minister Mantri unite to kill Kundan; their son is ambushed on the way to hospital and Meenu killed; Kundan is arrested on fabricated charges and nearly murdered.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is a revenge saga and a don's rise; the marriage is a fact of his success, not its motive.
chemistry_explanation: Film Information's trade review found that 'Emotions and romance have not been developed properly' and Pooja Batra 'unimpressive'; the pairing is given too little to establish itself.
actor_transformation: None documented; he becomes a husband and father in the course of becoming a don.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Kundan surrenders after destroying his enemies, and the film ends with a happy reunion at home.
relationship_analysis: The film splits the two sisters along the line of his career: Pooja is the home his violence threatens, Meenu the partner in it, and Meenu is the one who dies. Neither is a full character in the sources.
critical_reading: The trade press found the romance undeveloped. The wife's role is to worry, which the film registers and does nothing with.

initial_relationship: In love when the film begins; she is the daughter of his senior officer, ACP Amar Agnihotri
how_they_meet: Not documented.
courtship_pattern: Not documented beyond the established romance.
emotional_dynamic: Love broken by the apparent killing of her father and restored by his account of the truth.
pair_conflict: Under the undercover plan Arjun fires a blank at ACP Amar, but Amar is really killed in the ambulance; Kaajal is furious with him for killing her father until she hears the whole story.
pair_friction_explanation: Her fury is a real rupture between them, but it rests on a deception staged by others, and it ends as soon as she hears his account.
external_opposition_explanation: The jailer Lankeshwar and his allies in the police and the ministry turn a staged shooting into a real murder, trap Arjun in prison as her father's killer, and kill his father and have his sister gang-raped.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is established and then tested, but the role is the patriotic officer and one-man army; Film Information singled out his acting, action and dances.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Film Information praises each separately, Shetty for his acting, action and dances and Raveena Tandon as pretty and able, without commenting on the pair; the score is held at the midpoint.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: From a daughter who believes her lover killed her father to his ally against the men who did.
relationship_outcome: Not documented beyond her decision to forgive and help him; the film ends with Arjun hanging Lankeshwar.
relationship_analysis: The only pairing in the batch whose friction is generated from outside: the villains make Arjun appear to have killed her father. Her choice to believe him and help is the one decisive romantic act in the film, and it is hers.
critical_reading: No review discusses the pairing. Her forgiveness is quick, and it is offered on his word alone; the film needs her as an ally more than as a judge.

actress_prominence: Female lead and protagonist; the story is seen from her point of view (Rediff)
initial_relationship: Strangers, each the child of a corrupt parent
how_they_meet: Panna meets Aditya, son of the industrialist P. N. Patel (Rediff); the circumstances are not documented.
who_initiates: Unclear; Aditya introduces Panna to the basti behind his father's mill and to his old teacher, Joshi master (Rediff)
courtship_pattern: A bond over corrupt lineages; they find solace in the slum with Joshi master and the poet Bhau, to their parents' dismay, and become lovers. A car accident leaves him presumed dead, and she loses his unborn child.
emotional_dynamic: Two children of power who 'share a void of faith' (Rediff) and find in each other, and in the basti, a refuge from their parents.
pair_conflict: After the accident he joins a militant gang and has her kidnapped to force her mother to free a gang member; they reunite in captivity and piece together the years apart.
pair_friction_explanation: Kidnapping his former lover to pressure her mother is a coercive act aimed at her, even if the summary records an immediate reconciliation; it is the one serious breach, and it originates with him.
external_opposition_explanation: Both parents oppose the relationship, a car accident separates the lovers and costs Panna their child, and the parents later join forces in a corrupt alliance; the lovers end by killing them and, the article implies, themselves.
lover_boy_explanation: She is his soulmate and their love is the film's emotional spine, but his identity is political revolt; India Today notes 'very little of Gulzar's soothing brand of romance'.
chemistry_explanation: India Today captions the two leads 'Sunil Shetty and Tabu: sensitive portrayals', and Rediff and the Deccan Herald both describe her finding a 'soulmate' in him; the reviews praise both performances, though none discusses the chemistry directly.
actor_transformation: From the disaffected heir to a militant who kidnaps the woman he loved, and then her partner in a final act against their parents.
female_transformation: From a rebellious daughter watching her mother's rise to a woman who carries out 'poetic justice' against her.
relationship_outcome: Reunited during the kidnapping; together they slip into an election rally of Malti Barve and P. N. Patel and detonate bombs, destroying it. The article's wording ('explode bombs attached to them') implies the lovers die too.
relationship_analysis: Shetty's first off-mainstream role, and the batch's most serious romance: a love affair that is also a shared political position, and in which the woman is the protagonist. It is the only pairing of the batch in which friction comes from the hero's own coercion, and the only one in which the couple acts together against the world to the end.
critical_reading: The contemporary press praised the two performances and found the film either powerful (Rediff, Deccan Herald) or tediously abstract (Film Information). Read now, the ending, two lovers bombing their parents at a rally, is a startling endorsement of political violence that the film presents as justice; Cinestaan's 2019 retrospective judged it a didactic diatribe.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is a waitress at a restaurant he visits
how_they_meet: Unable to tip the waitress Piya, Ram promises to pay her the next day or, if his lottery ticket wins, to share the prize with her equally.
who_initiates: Not documented; the closeness is mutual
courtship_pattern: He wins Rs 5 crore and insists on giving her Rs 2.5 crore. As his wife chases fame, he and his neglected daughter find comfort in Piya's company; 'Their agonies draw them closer and mutual respect binds them' (Deccan Herald).
emotional_dynamic: Mutual respect and consolation; Piya 'adores Ram for his goodness', and she has a sad past of her own.
pair_conflict: None documented between them; the obstacle is his marriage.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between them is recorded; the review stresses mutual respect.
external_opposition_explanation: Ram is married, and his wife Manthara fights the payment and, once Piya's past is revealed, her 'tantrums take a murky twist'; the review calls what follows 'a painful path to love and reality'.
lover_boy_explanation: A married man's late romance, tender rather than ardent: the Deccan Herald credits him with 'a dignified passion'. His defining trait is integrity, and the love grows out of a kept promise.
chemistry_explanation: The Deccan Herald's review finds the love story 'laced with such rarified poignancy that it makes the whole experience enriching', and describes Shetty's 'dignified passion' against Priya Gill's serenity, 'a frozen beauty, as if waiting for events to thaw the ice': warm on him, cooler on her.
actor_transformation: From a husband starved of affection to a man who finds love with the woman to whom he kept his word.
female_transformation: Not documented beyond the revelation of her past.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the review speaks only of 'a painful path to love and reality'.
relationship_analysis: The batch's most central romance, and the only one built on conversation and consolation rather than on danger. It is also an adulterous attachment that the film licenses by making the wife monstrous, which is why its friction is so low and its opposition so high.
critical_reading: The Deccan Herald admired its leisurely elegance. The film's moral arithmetic depends on Manthara: a married man's love for a younger woman is made blameless by loading every vice onto his wife.

actress_prominence: Supporting; the hero's wife and the film's obstacle
initial_relationship: Married, with a young daughter
how_they_meet: Not documented.
courtship_pattern: Not applicable; the marriage predates the film.
emotional_dynamic: Her 'lust for money and fame' against his 'little wants' (Deccan Herald); she neglects husband and daughter.
pair_conflict: Money: she forces him to buy the lottery ticket, then fights his promise to give Piya half the prize, and is taken in by Manubhai's film talk.
pair_friction_explanation: The marriage is the film's open conflict: a wife who 'puts money above everything else, including her husband and their little daughter', and a husband who refuses her on the one point that matters to her.
external_opposition_explanation: The fraud Manubhai Shroff feeds Manthara's ambitions with film-star names, but the marriage's trouble is between the spouses.
lover_boy_explanation: No romantic feeling for his wife is documented.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The marriage is written as antagonism, with Archana Puran Singh's Manthara a figure of greed and comedy, so any warmth between them would work against the film's design.
actor_transformation: Her neglect drives him toward Piya.
female_transformation: Not documented; the review says only that her tantrums 'take a murky twist'.
relationship_outcome: Not documented.
relationship_analysis: The counterweight to PAIR-015: almost all the film's pair friction sits in the marriage, almost none in the new love. Manthara has the most independent goals of any woman in the film, money and a Bollywood career, and the film treats them as vices.
critical_reading: The Deccan Herald calls her 'This ravenous, despicable woman', which is how the film asks her to be seen. Read now, it is a familiar device: the wife made monstrous so the husband's turn to another woman needs no defence.

initial_relationship: House guest and his host's wife
how_they_meet: Kaalkeshwar introduces Arjun to his wife when he invites his rescuer to stay at his estate.
courtship_pattern: Not described; the summary says only that the guest and the wife 'have begun an affair' under the husband's roof.
emotional_dynamic: A subdued, submissive wife and the stranger who saved her husband's life; the affair is the one documented act of will by a woman otherwise defined by her husband's control.
pair_conflict: None documented between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between the lovers is recorded; every danger comes from the husband.
external_opposition_explanation: She is married to a pathologically jealous mob boss who once killed a man merely for shaking her hand and complimenting her, and the summary ends with his 'unimaginable' anger at learning of the affair. The threat is lethal, though the outcome is not documented.
lover_boy_explanation: An avenger whose first love died before the story begins, he becomes a lover who risks his life for another man's wife; the affair drives the second half, but the role's documented identity is still the gunman.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. No review of the film was located at all. The pairing of an action hero with a submissive wife in a jealous don's house is a stock set-up, and nothing documents how it plays; the score is held at the midpoint.
actor_transformation: Turns the grieving avenger into a lover again, the role's only documented change.
female_transformation: From a subdued, submissive wife to a woman who risks her husband's lethal jealousy; what follows is not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the Wikipedia summary ends when Kaalkeshwar learns of the affair.
relationship_analysis: The romance is the plot's engine: the gangster's possessive jealousy, established by the man he killed for a handshake, is a loaded gun, and the affair pulls the trigger. Arjun's earlier love, Maria, exists only as a dead motive, the pattern of batch 1 where the heroine's death authorises the hero's violence. Jealousy is marked Partial because it belongs to the husband rather than to the couple.
critical_reading: No contemporary review was located. Read now, the wife is defined almost entirely as her husband's property, and the summary gives no sign of her own wishes beyond the affair; the film's framing appears to treat adultery as rescue rather than betrayal, since the husband is the villain.

initial_relationship: His good friend Raj's sister
how_they_meet: Through her brother Raj, Karan's friend; no first meeting is described.
courtship_pattern: She makes overtures; he does not respond, because, in Film Information's words, 'he is burdened by the fact that he is guardian to five sisters'. The romantic songs are staged as dream sequences, which the trade review counts as a drawback.
emotional_dynamic: Her open pursuit against his duty-bound restraint; the romance exists mostly in fantasy numbers.
pair_conflict: His refusal to respond to her while his sisters remain unmarried.
pair_friction_explanation: The only documented tension is his refusal to reciprocate, a matter of duty rather than hostility; no quarrel between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: His guardianship of five sisters is what stops him, and the families are set at odds when her brother secretly marries his sister against his wishes, a marriage Karan resents as a humiliation.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is organised around fraternal protectiveness; Film Information writes that 'Romance is absent almost completely', and his romantic side is confined to dream songs.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Film Information's only comment on the romance is that it is 'absent almost completely' and that the dream-sequence songs are a drawback, which assesses the track's weakness rather than the pair. A romance confined to fantasy numbers is scored just below the midpoint.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented.
relationship_analysis: The remake keeps the Hitler premise of a brother who sacrifices his own romance to his sisters' marriages; here the heroine pursues and the hero withholds. The romance therefore tests his character rather than developing a relationship, and the trade review shows the Hindi version thinning it further.
critical_reading: Film Information found the whole film 'dated' for its 'regressive story', especially a brother who forbids his sisters to speak to boys. The heroine's pursuit is the film's only female initiative in love, and it is left unanswered on the evidence available.

actress_prominence: Female lead; 'the life of the enterprise' (Taran Adarsh); 'the best role of her career' (Screen)
initial_relationship: Lovers across a class divide: she is a rich businessman's daughter, he is poor and illegitimate
how_they_meet: Not shown; they are already a couple when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: First a mutual love that her father vetoes; then, three years after her marriage, Dev returns rich and 'pursues her through all available means', ruining her husband when she refuses him.
emotional_dynamic: Shared devotion turns into his possessive demand against her loyalty to the husband she has come to love.
pair_conflict: Her choice of her family, and later her husband, over him, and his refusal to accept it.
pair_friction_explanation: The rupture is hers: she leaves him to spare her parents, and he vows 'to destroy everything she holds dear'. After her marriage he hounds her and wrecks her husband's business, and she begs him to leave her alone. Their early love was frictionless, which keeps this below 9.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father rejects the poor, unshaven suitor, threatens suicide if she leaves, and marries her off; Dev's mother dies of the shock. In the second half her marriage is the obstacle.
lover_boy_explanation: Love is the whole of Dev's motivation, from defiant suitor to scorned millionaire to the man who finally lets her go. It is a lover's role curdled into obsession, which Film Information compared with Shah Rukh Khan's in Darr; the devotion is real, but it is no longer the pure lover-boy type.
chemistry_explanation: Taran Adarsh called Shetty's performance one of his best, 'especially the scenes between Sunil and Shilpa are fabulous', and Screen's review describes the pair as 'madly in' love. Screen also found the director had 'cold feet' about the grey role, so the sourced praise is for the early romance rather than the vendetta.
actor_transformation: Loss turns the poor lover into a vindictive tycoon; the husband's unconditional love finally turns him back towards decency.
female_transformation: From a dutiful daughter who gives him up to a wife who chooses her husband and confronts her ex-lover.
relationship_outcome: She stays with Ram; Dev lets her go and marries Sheetal.
relationship_analysis: The film's centre and the batch's key pairing. The lover is denied by class and a father's veto, the classic external obstacle, but the second half turns the hero into the obstacle. Dev's scorned love produces exactly the friction the 1990s action romances lacked, and it won Shetty the Filmfare Best Villain award while the film kept him nominally a hero. Film Information's objection that 'his deeds are anything but heroic' captures the film's unresolved double framing.
critical_reading: The film frames Dev's stalking and sabotage as the pain of a wronged lover, redeemed by the husband's forgiveness. Read now, it is the harassment of a married woman who has plainly refused him, and the resolution rewards him with another woman's devotion.

actress_prominence: Second female lead; nominated for Filmfare Best Supporting Actress
initial_relationship: Business partners
how_they_meet: Not documented; she is his partner after he becomes rich.
who_initiates: Sheetal (she adores him); Dev decides on the marriage at the end
courtship_pattern: She loves him while he pursues Anjali, and objects when he allies with Ram's step-family; he marries her once he gives Anjali up.
emotional_dynamic: Her devotion and moral check against his obsession with another woman.
pair_conflict: His vendetta, which she opposes.
pair_friction_explanation: She objects to his alliance with the in-laws; otherwise no quarrel is described.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is his fixation on Anjali; nothing outside the pair opposes them.
lover_boy_explanation: With Sheetal he is the beloved, not the lover; the marriage is a resolution, not a courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Film Information wrote only that Mahima Chaudhry 'looks tired and lacks glamour' though her 'performance is good'. A pairing that exists as her devotion and his last-minute decision is scored below the midpoint.
actor_transformation: Choosing her marks his acceptance of loss.
female_transformation: Not documented beyond her objection to his scheme.
relationship_outcome: Married at the end.
relationship_analysis: Sheetal is the consolation the film awards its redeemed anti-hero: a woman who loves him without condition and whose objection to his vendetta is the only moral voice at his side. The resolution keeps the romantic hero intact by pairing him off.
critical_reading: Read now, the marriage is a narrative tidy-up rather than a relationship: she is given to the man who spent the film pursuing another woman, and her love is the reward for his giving up.

actress_prominence: Top-billed actress but 'a minuscule role' (Film Information); 'wasted in a meaningless part' (Rediff)
initial_relationship: Village sweethearts
how_they_meet: Not documented; he falls in love with her in the village.
courtship_pattern: He loves her but marries his mentor's pregnant daughter to save her from disgrace; his wife and her brother try to drive Sudha out of the village. In Bombay, Sudha, now a police inspector, helps him after the gang attack, and he finally agrees to marry her.
emotional_dynamic: A steadfast love deferred by his chivalry; she waits and then helps him.
pair_conflict: None between them; his sense of honour separates them.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel is documented; the separation is his duty-bound choice, not a conflict with her.
external_opposition_explanation: His marriage to Pushpa bars the way, Pushpa and her brother try to expel Sudha from the village, and the threat of public ridicule is what forces the marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: He is a chivalrous one-man army first; the love story is a frame around the action, as Film Information's synopsis puts it.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Both reviews say her role is too small to register ('minuscule', 'wasted'), and Rediff found her 'more a Vanity Fair model' than a cop. With so little screen time together, the pairing is scored below the midpoint.
actor_transformation: Not documented beyond his decision to marry her.
female_transformation: From a village girl to a police inspector who joins the neighbourhood's attack on the gang.
relationship_outcome: He agrees to marry her.
relationship_analysis: The romance follows a pattern of chivalric self-denial: the hero sacrifices his love to save another woman's honour and is rewarded once that obligation is removed by her death. Sudha's police uniform gives her some function in the climax, but both reviews agree the film gives her little to do.
critical_reading: The framing treats his marriage of honour as nobility, and her waiting as fidelity. Read now, the woman with a profession is the least developed of the film's three women.

actress_prominence: Second female lead; 'Namrata has a meaty part, both in terms of footage and quality' (Rediff)
initial_relationship: Daughter of his Bombay host
how_they_meet: Her father Nanda welcomes Govind and his sister 'with open arms' when they arrive in Bombay.
courtship_pattern: The summary says only that they 'fall in love'; he ends by marrying Sudha.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented; Rediff's 'Our sympathies lie with Namrata' implies she is the one left behind.
pair_conflict: Not documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: His prior love for Sudha, who returns to help him, is the documented obstacle.
lover_boy_explanation: A romance in the Bombay section of an action film, given no documented courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Rediff gives her the best part of the three actresses and Film Information says she 'looks good and acts with conviction', but neither assesses her scenes with Shetty.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; Govind marries Sudha.
relationship_analysis: Gitika is the city romance that the village romance overrides. The reviews suggest the film gave her more footage than Sudha while still resolving the hero's love life in Sudha's favour.
critical_reading: Rediff's sympathy for Namrata reads as a contemporary complaint that the film discarded the heroine it had developed.

initial_relationship: His mentor's daughter
how_they_meet: Through her father, Govind's mentor.
who_initiates: Govind (he marries her to save her from public ridicule)
courtship_pattern: None; a marriage of honour after a police officer impregnates and abandons her.
emotional_dynamic: His chivalric duty against her contempt: she does not love him and hates Sudha 'with passion'.
pair_conflict: Her hatred of the marriage and of Sudha, and her infidelity.
pair_friction_explanation: She does not love him, schemes with her brother to drive out the woman he loves, and is unfaithful; the marriage is antagonistic throughout, short of open violence between the spouses.
external_opposition_explanation: Public disgrace forces the marriage, and her own brother poisons her when he discovers her infidelity.
lover_boy_explanation: A husband by obligation, with no romantic identity in the marriage.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. A loveless marriage of honour, scored low.
actor_transformation: The marriage separates him from Sudha; after Pushpa's death he leaves for Bombay.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: She is poisoned by her brother.
relationship_analysis: The marriage exists to prove the hero's honour: he takes on another man's disgrace and is repaid with contempt and betrayal, which the plot then removes by having her own brother kill her. It is the batch's clearest case of a woman's death clearing the hero's path, a device batch 1 used repeatedly.
critical_reading: Read now, the film punishes the 'fallen' woman twice, through pregnancy outside marriage and through her brother's poison, while the hero's sacrifice is celebrated.

actress_prominence: Female lead in a double role (Tina and Sweety)
initial_relationship: Boyfriend and girlfriend
how_they_meet: Not documented; already a couple.
courtship_pattern: Not described; he serves as the twins' accomplice once they swap places.
emotional_dynamic: A supportive, comic boyfriend in service of the heroine's plan.
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement is described.
external_opposition_explanation: The family's troubles are the plot, but nothing is shown blocking the couple themselves.
lover_boy_explanation: Filmfare calls him her 'love interest', but the part is comic support for the twin plot.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Filmfare and Film Information praise his comic timing and Kajol's double role separately but not their scenes together; the score is held at the midpoint.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented within the pairing.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; still together.
relationship_analysis: For the first time in the filmography the woman leads and Shetty supports: Tina drives the plot, and Sameer's job is to help. The reviews' praise for his restraint and timing marks this as one of the comic turns of 2000–2001 that broadened his image.
critical_reading: An unremarkable, healthy background romance; the twins' scheme to reunite their parents is the film's emotional business.

actress_prominence: Female lead in a double role
initial_relationship: Bodyguard and the married woman he is hired to protect
how_they_meet: Her husband hires Sagar to watch his depressed wife; he shadows her and rescues her from a suicide attempt.
courtship_pattern: Friendship after the rescue; her fondness grows into love and she proposes. He 'is unable to take a decision', and she kills herself. In Goa he meets her exact double, Pari, and with her help uncovers the conspiracy.
emotional_dynamic: Her dependency on her protector against his professional reserve and hesitation.
pair_conflict: His failure to answer her proposal, which precipitates her death.
pair_friction_explanation: The decisive moment between them is a rejection, or at least a hesitation, that the reviews say drives her to suicide; there is no recurring quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: She is married to the tycoon who hired him, and both reviews describe a criminal conspiracy in which Sagar was made a pawn.
lover_boy_explanation: The first half is a romantic drama ('He is very good, both, in action and romantic scenes'), but he is the hesitant beloved, not the pursuer, and the second half is an investigation.
chemistry_explanation: Film Information judged him 'very good... in romantic scenes' and wrote that Raveena Tandon 'does justice to her role', but also that there 'was no need to interweave the romantic angle with the suspense angle'. The sourced praise is for his romantic scenes rather than the pairing as such.
actor_transformation: Her death shatters him and turns the bodyguard into an investigator.
female_transformation: Not documented; her lookalike's identity is the mystery.
relationship_outcome: Not documented.
relationship_analysis: A Vertigo-like structure: the protector falls for a fragile married woman, loses her to apparent suicide, and meets her double. It reverses his usual role, since the woman proposes and his hesitation is the wound. Because no fetched source reveals the twist, how far the romance was itself part of the conspiracy is unknown.
critical_reading: The film couples romance with a deception plot that, on the reviews, uses the woman's fragility as bait. Read now, the depiction of her mental illness as a 'psychic streak' triggered by rejection is crude.

initial_relationship: Strangers; love at first sight for him
how_they_meet: Not documented; Rediff calls it 'a perfect case of love at first sight for him'.
courtship_pattern: She turns him down to pursue medicine; he secretly sponsors her research in Scotland and pays a model to seduce and then abandon her so that she will turn to him; he later tries to break her engagement to Taj.
emotional_dynamic: Purchase against autonomy: he treats her as a deal, and she never chooses him.
pair_conflict: Her refusal, met with covert manipulation.
pair_friction_explanation: She rejects him, and he answers by orchestrating her heartbreak; the friction is hidden from her but structural.
external_opposition_explanation: Her love for Gaurav and her parents' choice of Taj stand between them, but the main obstacle is her own refusal.
lover_boy_explanation: Love is his motive, but he courts through money and proxies; Film Information calls him a 'sober businessman' with 'little scope to act', and Rediff 'obsessive'. Romantic centrality is high, lover-boy identity low.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Film Information found 'the sensitivity of a love story... totally missing' and Keerti Reddy 'a total loss'; Rediff gave him 'a miniscule role'. Neither assesses Yash and Isha together, and the reviews' general verdict on the romance places the pairing low.
actor_transformation: From a buyer of love to a man who accepts his mother's choice of bride.
female_transformation: From a student who refuses marriage to a woman who returns to the man who betrayed her for money; her own wishes are overridden in Film Information's reading of the climax.
relationship_outcome: She marries Gaurav; Yash is engaged to Rubaina.
relationship_analysis: The batch's starkest instance of the rich man who treats a woman as an acquisition. The film distributes its romantic hero across three men, and Shetty's is the paymaster, a part that, with Dhadkan and Khel, places him on the possessive side of the triangle.
critical_reading: Film Information objected at the time that the climax reduces the girl 'to being a purchasable commodity'. Read now, every man in the plot bargains over her, and her studies are the only choice that is clearly her own.

initial_relationship: Uncle and niece
how_they_meet: Family; he visits.
courtship_pattern: He reveals that he loves her and wants to marry her, 'much to Jo's dismay'; The Hindu singles out his face-to-face scene with her lover.
emotional_dynamic: An unwanted claim by an older relative against her chosen love.
pair_conflict: She does not want him.
pair_friction_explanation: Her dismay at an unwanted proposal is substantial, though no open quarrel is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Her love for Shakthi is the obstacle to his suit.
lover_boy_explanation: A suitor in a special appearance, defined by an unwanted claim.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The Hindu praises his confrontation with her lover, not any scene with Jo.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented for him; Jo and Shakthi reconcile.
relationship_analysis: His Tamil debut casts him as the obstacle in someone else's romance; his arrival coincides with the misunderstanding that separates the lovers in one branch of the forking plot.
critical_reading: The uncle–niece match draws on a South Indian marriage custom that the film treats as an unwelcome claim; Jo's dismay is the film's own framing.

actress_prominence: Female lead; 'brilliant as the elder daughter of the tenant' (Film Information)
initial_relationship: Would-be evictor and the tenant's elder daughter
how_they_meet: He arrives to evict her family from his late father's house.
courtship_pattern: No courtship: a running war of lawsuits, police complaints, goons and domestic sabotage, an attempt to marry her off to his policeman friend, and finally his own decision to marry her.
emotional_dynamic: Combative equals; she gives as good as she gets.
pair_conflict: The house.
pair_friction_explanation: Sustained antagonism: he files cases, moves in by force, creates nuisances and sends musclemen; she 'breathes fire' in their confrontations. It resolves only at the end.
external_opposition_explanation: His debts drive the conflict, the policeman's sister stalls the match he arranges for her, and her past in a mental asylum is held against her.
lover_boy_explanation: Film Information calls the film 'completely devoid of romance'; the marriage is a comic resolution, not a courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Film Information wrote that Mahima Chaudhry 'breathes fire in dramatic scenes of confrontation with Sunil Shetty', but also that the film is 'completely devoid of romance and emotions'. The sourced reading credits their sparring, not a love story.
actor_transformation: From an evictor to a husband who moves his own family into the disputed house.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: He decides to marry her and moves his mother and sister into the house.
relationship_analysis: The only rivals-to-lovers structure so far in the filmography, and it comes in a comedy. Film Information noticed the imbalance of a hero fighting a household of women ('an unequal fight'), which the marriage resolves by absorbing the opponent.
critical_reading: Read now, his methods (goons, forced entry) are harassment, and marriage is the comic solution to a property dispute; she remains the more forceful character.

initial_relationship: Next-door neighbours; she is a young widow living with her mother-in-law
how_they_meet: As neighbours.

emotional_dynamic: Her warmth towards the boy against the father's rigidity.
pair_conflict: His treatment of Rohan.

lover_boy_explanation: A father's role in which the romance is secondary to the father–son story.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Rediff found Neha 'perpetually confused and hurt' and him 'average'; neither review assesses their scenes together.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented.
relationship_analysis: The romance is the moral counterweight to the father's tyranny: the woman who sides with the child becomes the man's partner, a structure that frames the love story as part of his softening.
critical_reading: Taran Adarsh found the father's abuse 'a bit too hard to absorb'; the romance offers a softer frame without, on the evidence, giving Antara a story of her own.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the daughter of Suraj's father's friend

actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
