external_opposition_explanation: Nothing external opposes them; the danger is entirely him.
lover_boy_explanation: No romantic identity: he never returns her feelings.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Rediff calls him 'terribly miscast towards the end' and does not assess their scenes; a one-sided love that ends in murder is scored very low.
actor_transformation: None.
female_transformation: From a devoted subordinate to an investigator who suspects her superior, and is killed for it.
relationship_outcome: He murders her; her body is found the next day in Raj's house.
relationship_analysis: The batch's darkest pairing. Her unreturned love explains why she misses the obvious, and the reveal recasts every scene of their partnership. It sits with Dhadkan and Khel in the turn toward possessive or predatory men in 2000–2003.
critical_reading: The film uses a woman's love as the blind spot that lets a killer operate; Rediff's description of him as an officer 'with a penchant for stalking the victims he is meant to protect' names the pattern.

initial_relationship: Client and interior designer
how_they_meet: He hires her to redo the interior of his mansion.
courtship_pattern: He is pleasant to her and her mother; when she falls for his friend Rohan, he buys the police officer and both lawyers to have Rohan jailed for life, comforts her in their shared grief, and wins her consent to marry him.
emotional_dynamic: Predatory patronage disguised as friendship; she is 'oblivious to Dev's feelings' (Rediff).
pair_conflict: Concealed: he has destroyed the man she loves; it surfaces when ACP Rajveer exposes him.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no open quarrel until the exposure, but the relationship rests on his betrayal of her and of Rohan; once revealed, it is fundamentally destructive.
external_opposition_explanation: Her love for Rohan, and then the ACP's reopening of the case, which leads to a climax at the engagement ceremony.
lover_boy_explanation: Desire drives the plot, but the role is a schemer, 'an anti-hero' in Bollywood Hungama's words.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Rediff found Celina Jaitley 'does little to emote' and Bollywood Hungama that she 'needs to work on her acting abilities', while both praise Shetty; neither assesses them together.
actor_transformation: None; the exposure confirms what he was.
female_transformation: From a woman in love with Rohan to a grieving fiancée of the man who framed him.
relationship_outcome: Exposed at the engagement ceremony; the marriage is not documented to take place.
relationship_analysis: Khel repeats Dhadkan's turn, even down to the name Dev, as Rediff noticed, but without redemption: the rich suitor removes his rival by corruption and courts the grieving woman. Shetty produced it himself, which suggests he chose the possessive anti-hero as a vehicle.
critical_reading: The film frames him as the villain to be unmasked. Read now, the courtship of a grieving woman by the man who caused her grief is coercion by deception, and she is given no part in uncovering it.

actress_prominence: Female lead and protagonist; first-billed woman
initial_relationship: A villager she meets after settling in his remote village
how_they_meet: Drishti meets him after moving to the village following her break-up with Manav; the circumstances are not documented.
who_initiates: Neither; his crush is never declared and she is unaware of it.
courtship_pattern: None. He watches over her and fights the man who threatens her.
emotional_dynamic: Silent devotion on his side, unawareness on hers; Bollywood Hungama calls it 'a soft corner'.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement is recorded; the feeling is one-sided and unspoken.
external_opposition_explanation: The romance is blocked less by opposition than by her love for her former boyfriend Manav, with whom she is reunited, and by Mohit's death, revealed only at the end. Sunny and Rahul threaten her safety, not a relationship that never begins.
lover_boy_explanation: Devotion is his main trait, but it is silent, and his function in the thriller is suspect and protector.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The summary gives them little shared intimacy, and Bollywood Hungama finds his climactic reappearance 'convenient and unpersuasive', so the score is low.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: None from him; she ends reunited with Manav.
relationship_outcome: Never declared. After he saves her from Rahul, she learns that he had committed suicide; she is reunited with Manav.
relationship_analysis: A ghost-story variant of the protector-lover: Mohit's devotion is expressed entirely through violence on Drishti's behalf, and the film withholds whether he was alive in the scenes he shares with her. It continues the batch-2 run of one-sided attachments (12B, Baaz) in a benign key.
critical_reading: The film frames his crush as pathos, the damaged outsider who loves without hope. A modern reading finds nothing coercive in it, since he never presses his feelings on her, though the film still makes male violence the proof of love.

initial_relationship: Girlfriend per Wikipedia; next-door neighbour per Bollywood Hungama
how_they_meet: Not documented; Bollywood Hungama introduces her as his neighbour.
courtship_pattern: An initial scuffle and then a bargain: she will get him into the underworld, and he will feed her information about it.
emotional_dynamic: Her ambition drives him; Wikipedia says she 'has set her sights on the billions' and makes him change his mind.
pair_conflict: Her wish to nab a don against his wish to stay honest, and an early scuffle.
pair_friction_explanation: An initial scuffle, and her push to make him a criminal for her own ends, but they work as partners for most of the film.
external_opposition_explanation: The gangster Jindaal, whom Rahul kidnaps by mistake, and the captivity in Pakistan in which the premise lands them.
lover_boy_explanation: The comedy of the reluctant don comes first; the romance is a comic track.
chemistry_explanation: Rediff's Patcy N: 'Initially, Suniel and Raveena's comedy track falls flat as they clearly lack comic timing', though Tandon 'improves towards the end'. Bollywood Hungama singles out their club scene, in which she challenges him to fight a don, as one of the few jokes that land.
actor_transformation: Her ambition turns an honest heir into a would-be don.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the premise ends with them held captive in Pakistan.
relationship_analysis: Here the woman is the ambitious partner and he the reluctant one, a reversal of the rescuer-and-rescued pattern of his 1990s action roles, played as farce. The two sources disagree on whether the couple start together, so the courtship arc is uncertain.
critical_reading: The film plays her ambition for comedy: a policewoman who would make her man a criminal to make her own name. She has more drive than he does, which is unusual for his romances.

initial_relationship: Established girlfriend
how_they_meet: Not documented; they are already a couple when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: A cycle of his cheating and her forgiveness: he follows her to Cape Town and is pardoned 'for the nth time'.
emotional_dynamic: Her exasperation against his philandering, then his jealousy as she charms other men.
pair_conflict: His serial infidelity, and then her double-crossing of him over the jewels.
pair_friction_explanation: His repeated cheating sends her abroad, and after the heist she ditches him and the others and turns her charms on Prasad while Laloo seethes.
external_opposition_explanation: The police and the rival claimants to the jewels complicate the heist, but the couple's troubles are of their own making.
lover_boy_explanation: A Casanova whose courtship consists of begging forgiveness; romance drives the farce, but he is a philanderer rather than a devoted lover.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Rediff's open letter condemns the performances wholesale, counting Shetty among the 'non-actors' and Masumeh as a talent made to look foolish, so the score is low.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: From a wronged girlfriend to the schemer who outplays everyone.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the summary ends with Padma double-crossing her partners.
relationship_analysis: A rare Shetty romance in which the woman holds the power: the hero's infidelity is the comic premise, her double-crossing the plot engine, and his jealousy the joke.
critical_reading: Played as a sex farce, which Rediff found vulgar. A modern reading sees mutual exploitation rather than romance, with neither partner trustworthy.

initial_relationship: Bride; the film opens with their wedding (Rediff)
how_they_meet: Not documented.
courtship_pattern: None shown; the film opens on the marriage.
emotional_dynamic: A 'loving family', in Rediff's phrase, under siege once their son is taken.
pair_conflict: None documented; the BBC hints that Sana 'discovers' there is more to the situation than first appears.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel is recorded; the BBC's hint that she discovers more than she knew is the only sign of strain.
external_opposition_explanation: Shekhar kidnaps their son, makes them believe the boy is dead and claims him as his own.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is cop and father; the marriage is the opening scene.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The BBC finds Chopra unconvincing 'as a plain housewife and concerned mother', and Rediff reduces her part to 'three tasks', so the score leans low.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: None documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the summary ends with the hunt for Shekhar.
relationship_analysis: A wife in the Ransom template: she exists to grieve and to carry the secret of the boy's parentage. After the predatory roles of 2000–2004 it returns him to the protector-husband of the 1990s films.
critical_reading: Contemporary reviews treat her as a function, Rediff's 'three tasks' and the BBC's 'plain housewife and concerned mother'. The marriage is healthy as described; the film gives her no choice beyond telling Shekhar the truth.

initial_relationship: Estranged wife
how_they_meet: Not documented; they are married before the film begins.
who_initiates: He does; he is trying to persuade her to return.
courtship_pattern: Attempted reconciliation after they lost their unborn baby.
emotional_dynamic: His persistence against her withdrawal; Bollywood Hungama: 'Suniel wants to patch up with his wife Raima'.
pair_conflict: An incident that killed their unborn baby, and her plan to divorce him.
pair_friction_explanation: Estranged after the loss of their baby, with divorce in prospect; serious and ongoing, though no quarrel is described in detail.
external_opposition_explanation: Jamwal's men take her, Dan and the schoolchildren she is escorting hostage at the stadium.
lover_boy_explanation: Winning his wife back is his private motive, but the role is a cop in an anti-terror ensemble.
chemistry_explanation: Bollywood Hungama: 'Only the Sanju-Shilpa love story appears convincing, otherwise the romantic sequences of the remaining three pair looks contrived', a verdict that includes this couple. Rediff found Raima Sen's character 'unimaginably irritating' and thought Shetty 'could have totally been cut out of the film'.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: He rescues her and the children; whether they reconcile is not documented.
relationship_analysis: A marriage divided by grief rather than villainy, a kind of strain his roles seldom carry. The thriller resolves the danger, not the marriage.
critical_reading: Reviewers dismissed the track as filler. A modern reading notes that the film gives her grief no voice: she exists to be won back and then rescued.

actress_prominence: Female lead; one of the two suspects who narrate the story
initial_relationship: Member of the same circle of five Indian friends in London (Rediff's 'coterie of five wannabe musicians')
how_they_meet: Not documented.
who_initiates: He does, per Bollywood Hungama: he wants to marry her.
courtship_pattern: Obsessive devotion to a woman who may be using him.
emotional_dynamic: Bollywood Hungama: 'Rocker is an obsessed lover, wanting to marry Sim. Sim is a temptress.'
pair_conflict: Whether she is 'really taking Rocker for a ride' (Bollywood Hungama).
pair_friction_explanation: The suspicion that she is manipulating him runs through the story; no open quarrel is documented.
external_opposition_explanation: In the suspects' account the terrorist Murtaza Arzai kills Rocker and two friends on a boat. The account is invented, so the obstacle exists only inside the story they tell.
lover_boy_explanation: Obsessive love is his defining trait in the narrated story, but the role serves a heist mystery.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The reviews praise Dutta's seductiveness ('looks every inch a seductress') and fault Shetty for not adding 'much more value' to a pivotal role, which suggests an uneven pairing.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Unclear: the love story is part of an invented account, and at the end Rocker meets Sim and Pipi alive, a co-conspirator in the ruse.
relationship_analysis: The romance sits inside a lie. Everything reported of Rocker's obsession comes from the suspects' testimony, which the ending discredits, so the 2000–2004 obsessive-pursuit pattern here becomes part of a con.
critical_reading: The film frames Sim as the femme fatale and Rocker as her dupe; Rediff calls her 'a conniving sex goddess'. A modern reading notes that her agency is cast entirely as sexual manipulation.

actress_prominence: Female lead; paired with Salman Khan's Anand
initial_relationship: Fiancée, engaged with her father's approval
how_they_meet: Not documented.
who_initiates: Not documented; her father approves the engagement.
courtship_pattern: None shown; an arranged engagement.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented; she loves Anand.
pair_conflict: Her love for her patient Anand.
pair_friction_explanation: Her love for another man ends the engagement, but no quarrel is recorded; he releases her.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacle is her love for Anand; her father backs the engagement.
lover_boy_explanation: Incidental: an engaged man whose one documented act is to let her go.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. No review mentions Shetty, and the part is too slight to rate above low.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: Not documented in relation to him.
relationship_outcome: He tells Tanvi to go with Anand, ending the engagement.
relationship_analysis: The noble fiancé who steps aside, a stock love-triangle device. As in Kyun! Ho Gaya Na a year earlier, Shetty is the fiancé the real hero has to get past.
critical_reading: The film presents his withdrawal as generosity. It leaves Tanvi's choice to the men around her: her father picks Karan, and Karan hands her to Anand.

actress_prominence: Female lead; the only heroine, pursued by every male lead
initial_relationship: A friend in Dubai, posing as a paraplegic architect
how_they_meet: Not documented; he is already in her circle when Rocky arrives.
courtship_pattern: Deception: he fakes disability to win her sympathy and forges newspapers to destroy every rival.
emotional_dynamic: Her trust in a friend she believes disabled, against his calculated manipulation.
pair_conflict: None that she knows of until a gunfight exposes his deceit.
pair_friction_explanation: She never quarrels with him until she discovers the deceit; the dishonesty is his and hidden from her.
external_opposition_explanation: Rival suitors, Rocky, Tommy and above all Karan, compete for her throughout.
lover_boy_explanation: His whole role is the pursuit of Natasha, but as a comic schemer rather than a romantic hero.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Rediff's only remark on Shetty concerns his voice, and the BBC finds Rimi Sen 'no Cameron Diaz'; the score is low.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: From a trusting friend to a woman who learns that her admirers have lied to her.
relationship_outcome: Exposed when Karan tells her about his newspaper scams; she ends with Karan.
relationship_analysis: Played for farce, the pursuit uses the same tools as the 2000–2004 predatory roles: disguise, sabotage of rivals and manipulation of a woman who cannot see it. The film is a remake of There's Something About Mary.
critical_reading: The film treats faked disability and forged scandal as gags. A modern reading sees stalking and fraud played for laughs, and a heroine whose suitors all lie to her.

initial_relationship: Fiancée
how_they_meet: Not documented.
courtship_pattern: Engaged at the start; the wedding preparations in London frame the film.
emotional_dynamic: His trust against her concealed past with his best friend Danny.
pair_conflict: Her earlier involvement with Danny, kept from him.
pair_friction_explanation: Her concealment of her past with his best friend, and his heartbreak when she tells him; he forgives her.
external_opposition_explanation: Danny, her former lover and Kunal's best friend, used Kunal to get near her and still believes they can be together.
lover_boy_explanation: A trusting groom rather than a romantic hero; the romance is secondary to Anu and Aman's.
chemistry_explanation: Rediff's Sukanya Verma, on Ameesha Patel: 'Her romantic scenes with a heavily miscast Sunil Shetty make for agonising viewing. It's a how-not-to-act demonstration. In terms of chemistry, none of the actors share any vibes.'
actor_transformation: From a trusting groom to a man who forgives his bride's past.
female_transformation: She chooses honesty and tells Kunal about Danny.
relationship_outcome: Kunal chases Danny away and, persuaded by Aman, marries Shirani.
relationship_analysis: A rare Shetty role as the wronged party in a romance rather than the rival or the rescuer; the betrayal comes from his best friend, and the marriage survives it.
critical_reading: The film makes Danny the only villain and treats Shirani's silence as forgivable. Rediff's verdict on the pairing itself was among the harshest the batch received.

actress_prominence: Female lead; title role, paired with Abhishek Bachchan's Sultan
initial_relationship: A courtesan with whom he becomes infatuated
how_they_meet: Not documented; he comes into her life in Lucknow while Sultan is away.
courtship_pattern: Determined pursuit after rejection; per the BBC he buys her as the highest bidder.
emotional_dynamic: Infatuation on his side, rejection on hers; she uses his offer to reach Sultan.
pair_conflict: She rejects him and travels with him only to find Sultan.
pair_friction_explanation: She rejects his advances, and he lies to Sultan that they slept together, wrecking her reunion.
external_opposition_explanation: Her love for Sultan, and the soldiers who arrest him as a wanted dacoit.
lover_boy_explanation: A pursuer and spoiler rather than a lover-hero.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Rediff reserves 'scintillating chemistry' for Rai and Abhishek Bachchan, and the relationship is written as rejection, so the score is low.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: His lie costs her Sultan, a step in her decline.
relationship_outcome: Both are arrested, and his lie leads Sultan to send her back to Lucknow.
relationship_analysis: The obsessive rival of 2000–2004 returns in a prestige period adaptation; this time his weapon is slander rather than violence.
critical_reading: The BBC's account of a sale makes the coercion explicit. A modern reading sees a purchase and a lie, not a romance.

initial_relationship: Established lovers
how_they_meet: Not documented; she is already in love with Ram when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: A secret romance between a broke courier and a rich girl, sustained while he hunts for money.
emotional_dynamic: Steady mutual affection; he scrambles for money while she waits.
pair_conflict: None between them; the obstacle is money.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel between them is documented; they briefly 'decide to split ways' only when the money seems lost.
external_opposition_explanation: Her 'high society parents will never approve of marriage, not unless Ram has lots and lots of money', and her father arranges her marriage to Harbans's son, whose reception is held at the very hotel where the climax plays out.
lover_boy_explanation: Love motivates his scheme, but the role is driven by money and farce; the romance is a thread rather than his identity.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Bollywood Hungama finds Shetty 'natural to the core' but says the heroines 'don't have much to do', which limits the pair's screen time.
actor_transformation: From a broke dreamer to a man with the money to marry her (by luck rather than change).
female_transformation: None documented.
relationship_outcome: The couples recover the ransom suitcase together; a wedding is not described.
relationship_analysis: The 2009 Shetty romance in a comedy: a secondary couple whose only obstacle is her parents' snobbery, solved by a suitcase of money. He is neither possessive nor heroic here; the romance is a reason for the scheme, and the deception is aimed at her parents, not at her.
critical_reading: Contemporary reviews treat the romances as filler in a Priyadarshan farce. A modern reading sees a relationship whose legitimacy depends entirely on money, which the film plays for laughs rather than questions.

actress_prominence: Co-lead of one of three stories
initial_relationship: Married couple with a son
how_they_meet: Not applicable; married before the film opens.
courtship_pattern: No courtship; a marriage worn down by work, debt and parenting.
emotional_dynamic: Constant bickering that reviews frame as 'the meeting of minds'.
pair_conflict: His long working hours, their EMIs and their disagreements about raising their neglected son.
pair_friction_explanation: nowrunning describes 'marital discord'; a search summary of reviews calls them 'a constantly bickering married couple' who clash over his hours and their son.
external_opposition_explanation: The pressures of Mumbai life — working hours, loan instalments, a 'haphazard lifestyle' — wear at the marriage; no person opposes it.
lover_boy_explanation: A harried husband and father; romance is a matter of rebuilding a marriage, not courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Bollywood Hungama ranks the 'Suniel-Vidya track' second of the film's three stories: 'treated sensitively, but a few moments are plain ordinary, especially their initial portions'. nowrunning credits 'great chemistry' only to Nana Patekar and Dimple Kapadia.
actor_transformation: Bollywood Hungama's 'meeting of minds' suggests he learns to meet his wife halfway; the resolution is not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented; the stories merge after the interval around the café's legal fight.
relationship_analysis: Shetty's first married-couple drama, and a break from his 2000s pattern of possessive or criminal men: the friction is the ordinary wear of work and money, and the film treats both partners as equals. With 2 Chehare, it is one of only two pairings in this batch where the romance is the subject rather than a side thread.
critical_reading: Bollywood Hungama found the track sensitive but uneven in its opening stretch and praised Shetty's maturity; nowrunning saved its praise for the older couple. A modern reading credits it with a realistic picture of an urban marriage under financial strain, with blame assigned to neither side.

initial_relationship: Married couple
how_they_meet: Not applicable; married before the film opens.
courtship_pattern: No courtship; his cheating, her discovery, and an eventual reconciliation.
emotional_dynamic: Her suspicion and vigilance against his clumsy infidelity.
pair_conflict: His serial affairs, which she has already begun to expose through a friend and later through the detective Kishan.
pair_friction_explanation: His infidelity is the premise; Maya has a 'secret best friend' who exposes him, and when his partners tip her off to his hotel date the marriage breaks into open conflict.
external_opposition_explanation: The detective Kishan and Yogi's own partners, who betray him to save themselves, accelerate the exposure; the trouble itself comes from within the marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: A philanderer; he courts other women, not his wife.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Sinema.SG calls Yogi 'perhaps the least skillful of the lot' at cheating, and nowrunning faults Celina Jaitly's make-up rather than the pair's interplay.
actor_transformation: From a careless cheat to a chastened husband.
female_transformation: From a suspicious wife to one who forgives.
relationship_outcome: Yogi and Maya reconcile at the end.
relationship_analysis: The comic counterpart to Padmashree Laloo Prasad Yadav (PAIR-037): the hero's infidelity is the joke and the wife is the one with information and leverage. The film punishes the husbands and then restores the marriages, a convention that makes the reconciliation automatic rather than earned.
critical_reading: Reviewers judged the film a weak sex comedy. A modern reading sees the wives' surveillance as the film's only form of agency, and the happy ending as a reset in which the husbands' behaviour is forgiven rather than examined.

initial_relationship: Not documented (a college romance is implied by the love songs)
how_they_meet: Not documented.
courtship_pattern: A conventional romance told through 'a few love songs', ending in marriage.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented beyond his being 'a romantic'.
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is documented; the romance runs straight to marriage.
external_opposition_explanation: 'A chain of events' kills Ajay 'minutes before his suhaag raat', leaving Radha a widow who is later offered another groom; the cause of death is not given in the review.
lover_boy_explanation: Ajay is defined as a romantic and a model brother, with love songs to prove it; the second half belongs to the thug Babu, which dilutes the archetype.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Mumbai Mirror mocks the love songs as 'choreographed by PT teachers', which suggests little charge between the leads.
actor_transformation: None; the character dies.
female_transformation: From bride to widow facing a second marriage.
relationship_outcome: Ajay dies minutes before their wedding night; Radha is later to remarry.
relationship_analysis: A 1990s production released in 2015, and it shows: the romance is the earlier Shetty pattern in which the beloved is a reason for violence, but reversed — here the hero dies and the woman survives. The double role lets the film keep its star after killing the lover.
critical_reading: Mumbai Mirror treated the film as an embarrassing relic. A modern reading has little to work with: Radha exists as bride and widow, with her own choices undocumented.

initial_relationship: Married, with a teenage daughter, before the film begins
how_they_meet: Not shown.
courtship_pattern: None; a long marriage in its final stage.
emotional_dynamic: Hostile and unequal: a philandering, misogynistic husband and a 'long-suffering' wife; they 'yell at each other for two minutes straight' (Mint).
pair_conflict: His affair with the younger Anahita, who becomes pregnant.
pair_friction_explanation: The conflict is his own infidelity and contempt: the marriage is 'acrimonious' (The Hindu), the parents 'aren't exactly the best of friends' (Indian Express), and it ends in divorce. Short of 9 only because no coercion or violence is documented.
external_opposition_explanation: Almost nothing outside the couple works on them: Hindustan Times mentions a 'patriarchal grandfather' in the broken-family track. The mistress is not counted here, because the affair is the husband's own choice.
lover_boy_explanation: No romantic identity: he is a cheating father whose only documented warmth is for his daughter's suitor.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Mint singles out their two-minute shouting match among the film's 'strange, disjointed scenes', and India Today says the pair are used 'to add melodrama', which suggests performers hitting their marks rather than playing a marriage with any history.
actor_transformation: None documented.
female_transformation: From long-suffering wife to leaving with her daughter.
relationship_outcome: After Pia learns of the affair and the pregnancy on Diwali, Neelu takes her to her maternal home, and the couple head for divorce.
relationship_analysis: The last pairing in the filmography inverts the first. The 1990s hero fought villains and fathers for the woman; here Shetty plays the father, as the philandering patriarch whose affair is the wound behind his daughter's love story. It extends the husbands-under-strain line of Tum Milo Toh Sahi and Thank You, but where Thank You played the cheating husband for laughs, Nadaaniyan plays him straight, as melodrama.
critical_reading: Reviews treated the parents as padding: Hindustan Times found him 'wasted', and India Today questioned using the pair 'to add melodrama'. The film frames his misogyny and infidelity as damage done to Pia, and a modern reading would add that Neelu exists mainly as a sufferer whose own wishes go undescribed. Film Information's claim that the couple had long been separated conflicts with the plot and is not followed.
